text.tspan: Canonicity
What is “Canon”?
Canonicity
The reader may be asking him or herself, “Why is there a section of the
introduction to 1 and 2 Peter dedicated to the discussion of Canonicity?
What does that have to do with 1 and 2 Peter?” I assure you, it has
everything to do with 1 and 2 Peter. Often
overlooked but deeply
important to the question of authorship for
each
of the NT books,
especially those whose authorships are questioned by many scholars, is
the question of canonicity. What is its importance? The issue of canon
is one that has to do with
authority
. If the canon is “a closed list of
authoritative, sacred texts” coming from apostolic figures (such as
Matthew, John, etc.) and holds their authority (given to them by Jesus),
then the question of canon is deeply connected with the question of
authorship.
Let me say it in another, simpler, and more straightforward
way, “If Peter is not the author of 1 and 2 Peter, then why is it in our
New Testament canon? Can these letters hold divine authority without
being apostolic? If so, when (and how) were they give
n that authority?
And if it should not be in our New Testament canon, then should we be
reading it as if it was divinely inspired and has the same authority as the
actually
divinely
inspired books of the canon?
” This is a serious
question. There is yet another question we must ask,
Did the church
fathers get it wrong?”
What is “Canon”?
What is “Canon”?
Before talking more
specifically about the canonicity of 1 and 2 Peter, I
would like to back up and explain what this discussion is about; namely,
what
is
“canon”? The very first thing someone needs to know about the
discussion of canon in biblical scholarship is “that ‘much of the present
confusion over the problem of canon turns on the failure to reach an
agreement regarding the terminology.’”
Before continuing, I would like the reader to know I am by no
means covering everything that could be said about “canon.” I am
leaving many, many details out in hopes of offering a concise, only
the
. For my definition of “canon,” I am indebted to one of my undergraduate professors.
. Brevard Childs as qtd. in Michael J. Kruger,
Canon Revisited: Establishing the Origins and
Authority of the New Testament Books
(Wheaton, IL: Crossway, 2012), 27. For a detailed and
helpful analysis of different “canonical models” (that is, how people evaluate what should be part
of the NT), see in Kruger’s book,
Part 1: Determining the Canonical Model
